Key insight: Product dimensions vary clearly by category — large categories like furniture and office items show much bigger average dimensions (e.g., **Office Furniture length 55.63 cm, height 41.86 cm, width 37.92 cm**), while electronics and small accessories are much smaller (e.g., **Telephony length 18.43 cm, height 6.85 cm, width 13.25 cm**). This indicates a strong categorical separation in size rather than a single continuous relationship across all categories.

Interpretation:
- Product count is right-skewed with a few high-volume categories (outliers). The largest category is Bed/Bath/Table with **3,029** products and Sports/Leisure follows with **2,867** — these high counts can dominate any aggregate analysis.
- Categories associated with furniture, office equipment and luggage show the largest average linear dimensions:
  - Office Furniture: avg length **55.63 cm**, avg height **41.86 cm**, avg width **37.92 cm** (a clear size peak).
  - Furniture Living Room: avg length **50.73 cm**, avg width **44.43 cm**.
  - Luggage Accessories: high height/width (**29.58 cm**, **30.71 cm**).
- Small-item categories clustered at the low end of size:
  - Telephony: avg length **18.43 cm**, height **6.85 cm**, width **13.25 cm**.
  - Watches & Gifts and Perfumery also show small average dimensions.
- Because counts are highly skewed (mean product count **457.6**, median **99.5**, max **3,029**), simple averages across all products can be misleading; per-category averages are more meaningful here.
- This dataset shows clear grouping by category rather than a smooth numeric correlation between any single dimension and category count. To quantify the relationship, compute per-category correlation coefficients (e.g., Pearson or Spearman) between product count and each dimension or run a clustering/ANOVA to test whether dimension differences across categories are statistically significant.

The chart below illustrates the categorical separation of average length/height/width — larger furniture and home categories cluster at higher dimension values while electronics, telephony and accessories cluster at smaller values.
